title: Let him curse (2 Samuel 16:5–13)
hook: Shimei curses the fleeing king; David will not strike back
carry: one choice, on one road, to keep walking

segments.voice: Yesterday, David climbed the Mount of Olives, barefoot and head covered. Your line was he let the hard day be hard. Did you take a next step on a hard day? Today, on the far side of that hill, someone is waiting with stones. Day seven hundred fifty-three.
screen: `HE LET THE HARD DAY BE HARD.`

segments.voice: Stones. That's the first thing David's people notice at Bahurim: stones flying at them from the hillside. Then the voice. A man named Shimei, son of Gera, from the family of Saul, is walking along the ridge above the road, throwing rocks and dust and shouting. Get out, get out, you man of blood! The Lord has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, whose throne you took. Now the kingdom is your son's. Below him walks the king, his mighty men on his right hand and on his left.
screen: `STONES FROM THE HILLSIDE.` → `SHIMEI OF THE HOUSE OF SAUL.` → `YOU MAN OF BLOOD!`

segments.voice: Abishai, one of David's commanders, has heard enough. Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head. And David says no. His answer comes in layers. First: what have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Then: "let him curse", because maybe the Lord has told him to curse David, and who could then ask, why have you done so? Then the line that shows where David's mind really is: my own son, who came from my own body, is hunting for my life. How much more this man from Benjamin? Leave him alone, and let him curse. And finally a hope: maybe the Lord will look on my affliction, and repay me good for his cursing today. So they keep walking. And Shimei keeps pace with them along the hillside, cursing, throwing stones, flinging dust, for as long as the road runs beside the ridge. Notice what David is not saying. He doesn't say Shimei is right, and the narrator doesn't either. But David once heard Thou art the man, and some readers hear that in his answer: a king who knows he isn't innocent. So he lets an insult go by without needing to win it. There's an honest wrinkle, though. Much later, on his deathbed, David tells Solomon not to hold Shimei guiltless. The text keeps that too. The restraint on the road was real. It wasn't the whole of David. That makes the moment more useful, not less. Letting one insult go doesn't require being a saint. It requires one choice, on one road, to keep walking.
screen: `LET ME TAKE OFF HIS HEAD.` · then, large: `LET HIM CURSE.` · then: `MY OWN SON SEEKS MY LIFE.` · `MAYBE THE LORD WILL SEE MY AFFLICTION.` · `LATER, A DEATHBED ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one insult go. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a jab that's still in you: a comment in a meeting, a message from a relative, something a stranger shouted. Notice the Abishai in you, the part that wants to go over there and settle it. Thank it, and tell it to put the sword down. You don't have to agree with what was said. You just don't have to answer it. On each breath out, let the words fall behind you like dust on a road. If you pray, you can leave it with God. The bell holds the time.
Shimei. The man who threw stones and curses at David along the road, and was let alone. Today's word.
Your line: one choice, on one road, to keep walking. Today, when someone takes a shot at you, let one of them go by without a reply. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Jews read Shimei's cursing as part of the book of Samuel; the Talmud praises those who are insulted and do not insult back, and David on the road to Bahurim is one picture of that restraint.

fork.setup: you're David, fleeing your own son. a man on the ridge is cursing you and throwing stones, and your soldier offers to silence him. what do you say?
options: go, and take off his head.
fork.reveal: let him alone, and let him curse. David keeps walking, and Shimei keeps throwing stones along the hillside.

original.note: Hebrew: and let him curse, from David's answer in 2 Samuel 16:11.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saintly king who never held a grudge.
what it means: on that road, David chose not to answer an insult, perhaps knowing he wasn't innocent himself.
what a scholar hears: the deathbed charge in 1 Kings 2:8–9 shows the restraint was real but not the whole of David.
